records.title: Free fall in a uniform gravitational field
records.subject: Physics
records.shortDescription: Free fall is motion under gravity alone. In a near-Earth uniform field, a body released from rest accelerates downward at g.
records.ageAppropriateExplanation: Imagine letting go of a ball where air has no effect. It falls faster each second because Earth pulls it downward.
explanation: Free fall is motion under gravity alone. In a near-Earth uniform field, a body released from rest accelerates downward at g.
Taking downward as positive, v=gt and distance fallen=½gt², until ground contact. The model uses g=9.81 m/s²; it excludes air resistance and variation in gravity.
In an evacuated drop tube, objects of different masses released together have equal acceleration.
scientificPrinciples: Taking downward as positive, v=gt and distance fallen=½gt², until ground contact. The model uses g=9.81 m/s²; it excludes air resistance and variation in gravity.

definitions.Uniform field: A region where gravitational acceleration has the same magnitude and direction.

records.formula: v = gt; s = ½gt²; v² = 2gs · v m/s, s m, t s
realLifeExamples: In an evacuated drop tube, objects of different masses released together have equal acceleration.
objectives: Start at rest at the selected height.
Equal time intervals cover increasing distances.
Keep height fixed and compare two masses.
misconceptions: A heavier object does not have greater free-fall acceleration in this uniform-field model.

records.title: Air resistance
records.subject: Physics
records.shortDescription: Air resistance opposes a body’s velocity relative to air. For this falling-body model, drag increases with the square of speed.
records.ageAppropriateExplanation: Air pushes against a falling object. A wider object feels more resistance at the same speed.
explanation: Air resistance opposes a body’s velocity relative to air. For this falling-body model, drag increases with the square of speed.
For downward speed v, Fdrag=½ρCdAv² upward and acceleration=g−Fdrag/m. Air density and drag coefficient are fixed teaching assumptions.
A broad parachute slows descent by increasing frontal area; this model does not calculate deployment.
scientificPrinciples: For downward speed v, Fdrag=½ρCdAv² upward and acceleration=g−Fdrag/m. Air density and drag coefficient are fixed teaching assumptions.

definitions.Drag: Force resisting relative motion through a fluid.
definitions.Frontal area: Projected area facing the flow, measured in m².

realLifeExamples: A broad parachute slows descent by increasing frontal area; this model does not calculate deployment.
objectives: At zero speed, quadratic drag is zero.
Compare drag with weight.
A finite drop may end before terminal speed.
misconceptions: Air resistance is not constant, and it does not point upward for every possible direction of motion.

records.title: Terminal velocity
records.subject: Physics
records.shortDescription: Terminal velocity occurs when drag balances weight, so vertical acceleration becomes zero while the body continues moving.
records.ageAppropriateExplanation: A falling object can reach a steady speed when the air’s upward push balances its weight.
explanation: Terminal velocity occurs when drag balances weight, so vertical acceleration becomes zero while the body continues moving.
For a body falling in still air with quadratic drag and negligible buoyancy, vt=√(2mg/(ρCdA)). The solution approaches vt; a short tower may be insufficient.
Skydivers change posture to change area and hence terminal speed; the model represents a fixed posture.
scientificPrinciples: For a body falling in still air with quadratic drag and negligible buoyancy, vt=√(2mg/(ρCdA)). The solution approaches vt; a short tower may be insufficient.

definitions.Terminal speed: Steady limiting speed when the net force is zero.

realLifeExamples: Skydivers change posture to change area and hence terminal speed; the model represents a fixed posture.
objectives: Weight acts downward throughout descent.
At the limit, drag equals weight.
Compare mass and area separately.
misconceptions: Zero acceleration does not mean zero velocity.

steps.caption: At the limit, drag equals weight.
steps.detail: The acceleration approaches zero.

steps.caption: Compare mass and area separately.
steps.detail: Terminal speed scales as √m and 1/√A.

records.title: Buoyancy
records.subject: Physics
records.shortDescription: Buoyancy is the resultant upward pressure force exerted by a fluid on an immersed object.
records.ageAppropriateExplanation: Water pushes harder on the bottom of a submerged object than on its top, creating an upward force.
explanation: Buoyancy is the resultant upward pressure force exerted by a fluid on an immersed object.
In a stationary uniform-density fluid, Fb=ρfluid g Vdisplaced. A freely floating object balances weight with buoyancy; a held object may need another force.
A floating boat displaces enough water for the displaced water’s weight to equal the boat’s weight.
scientificPrinciples: In a stationary uniform-density fluid, Fb=ρfluid g Vdisplaced. A freely floating object balances weight with buoyancy; a held object may need another force.

definitions.Buoyancy: Net upward hydrostatic force on an immersed object.
definitions.Displaced volume: Volume of fluid excluded by the submerged part.

realLifeExamples: A floating boat displaces enough water for the displaced water’s weight to equal the boat’s weight.
objectives: Identify the submerged part.
Multiply fluid density, g and displaced volume.
At fixed volume, denser fluid produces more buoyancy.
misconceptions: Buoyancy depends on displaced volume and fluid density, not on object mass alone.

records.title: Archimedes principle
records.subject: Physics
records.shortDescription: Archimedes’ principle states that buoyant force equals the weight of the fluid displaced by an immersed body.
records.ageAppropriateExplanation: Imagine replacing the underwater part of an object with water. That water’s weight tells you the upward buoyant force.
explanation: Archimedes’ principle states that buoyant force equals the weight of the fluid displaced by an immersed body.
The principle follows from hydrostatic pressure forces. Displaced-fluid mass is ρV, and its weight is ρgV; partial and complete immersion use the same rule.
A ship’s hull can contain air while its total mass is supported by the water displaced by the submerged hull.
scientificPrinciples: The principle follows from hydrostatic pressure forces. Displaced-fluid mass is ρV, and its weight is ρgV; partial and complete immersion use the same rule.
realLifeExamples: A ship’s hull can contain air while its total mass is supported by the water displaced by the submerged hull.
objectives: Read its density in kg/m³.
Multiply density by displaced volume.
Double immersion before full submergence.
misconceptions: The displaced-fluid volume equals submerged object volume, not necessarily the entire object volume.

steps.title: Define the fluid
steps.caption: Read its density in kg/m³.
steps.detail: Density and volume must use compatible units.

steps.title: Find displacement
steps.caption: Use only the submerged volume.
steps.detail: A partially immersed block displaces less than its full volume.

steps.title: Find fluid mass
steps.caption: Multiply density by displaced volume.
steps.detail: The result has units of kilograms.

steps.title: Find fluid weight
steps.caption: Multiply displaced mass by g.
steps.detail: This equals the buoyant force.

steps.title: Test proportionality
steps.caption: Double immersion before full submergence.
steps.detail: Buoyancy doubles in the uniform liquid.

records.title: Apparent loss in weight
records.subject: Physics
records.shortDescription: A suspended object has a smaller support-force reading in a fluid because buoyancy provides part of the upward force.
records.ageAppropriateExplanation: A hanging scale pulls upward less strongly when water also supports the object.
explanation: A suspended object has a smaller support-force reading in a fluid because buoyancy provides part of the upward force.
At rest with upward support, T=mg−Fb. The apparent loss in weight is W−T=Fb. Negative support means a downward restraint is needed; an ordinary string cannot push down.
A dense stone suspended from a spring balance reads less when submerged.
scientificPrinciples: At rest with upward support, T=mg−Fb. The apparent loss in weight is W−T=Fb. Negative support means a downward restraint is needed; an ordinary string cannot push down.

definitions.Apparent weight: Support-force reading, not a change in gravitational mass.
definitions.Tension: Pulling force exerted by a taut string.

records.formula: T = mg − ρgVdisplaced; W − T = Fb
realLifeExamples: A dense stone suspended from a spring balance reads less when submerged.
objectives: Find W=mg.

misconceptions: Immersion does not reduce the object’s mass or its gravitational weight in the model.

records.title: Angle of contact
records.subject: Physics
records.shortDescription: Contact angle describes how a liquid surface meets a solid, measured through the liquid. It helps determine whether a narrow tube shows capillary rise or depression.
records.ageAppropriateExplanation: A liquid can curve upward or downward where it touches a wall. The angle at that meeting point matters.
explanation: Contact angle describes how a liquid surface meets a solid, measured through the liquid. It helps determine whether a narrow tube shows capillary rise or depression.
In an ideal cylindrical tube, h=2γcosθ/(ρgr). Angles below 90° give rise, above 90° give depression, and 90° gives no net capillary height in this model.
Clean water on glass commonly wets the wall; actual angles depend on surface chemistry and contamination.
scientificPrinciples: In an ideal cylindrical tube, h=2γcosθ/(ρgr). Angles below 90° give rise, above 90° give depression, and 90° gives no net capillary height in this model.

definitions.Contact angle: Angle between solid surface and liquid-interface tangent, measured through the liquid.
definitions.Wetting: Tendency of a liquid to spread over or adhere to a solid.

records.formula: h = 2γ cosθ / (ρgr) · θ in degrees in the controls
realLifeExamples: Clean water on glass commonly wets the wall; actual angles depend on surface chemistry and contamination.
objectives: Identify solid, liquid and gas.
An angle below 90° gives positive height.
The equation predicts equilibrium height.
misconceptions: Contact angle is measured through the liquid, and it is not always zero.

records.title: Ionic bonding
records.subject: Chemistry
records.shortDescription: Ionic bonding is electrostatic attraction among oppositely charged ions, commonly arranged in an extended crystal.
records.ageAppropriateExplanation: Sodium can form Na⁺ and chlorine can form Cl⁻. In solid salt, each ion attracts several oppositely charged neighbours.

Formal electron transfer tracks charge bookkeeping: Na loses one electron and Cl gains one. An interior ion in rock-salt NaCl has six nearest opposite-charge neighbours; the isolated pair potential here is not a full crystal-energy calculation.
Table salt is an extended NaCl crystal, not a collection of isolated NaCl molecules.

records.subject: Chemistry
records.shortDescription: A catalyst offers a different reaction pathway and increases the rate without being consumed overall.
records.ageAppropriateExplanation: A catalyst helps a reaction proceed faster; it does not make equilibrium favour products just by speeding both directions.

records.title: Effect of change in temperature
records.subject: Chemistry
records.shortDescription: Temperature changes reaction rates by changing rate constants; many reactions proceed faster at higher temperature.
records.ageAppropriateExplanation: At higher temperature, a greater fraction of collisions can reach the energy needed for the modeled pathway.
explanation: Temperature changes reaction rates by changing rate constants; many reactions proceed faster at higher temperature.
The Arrhenius equation k=Aexp(−Ea/RT) uses absolute temperature in kelvin. The chosen A and Ea are constant across the control range; real mechanisms and phases can change outside a limited range.
Food spoils more slowly when cooled because many chemical and biological processes slow; this model does not predict food safety.

records.title: Activation energy
records.subject: Chemistry
records.shortDescription: Activation energy is the energy-scale parameter in the Arrhenius relation for a reaction pathway.
records.ageAppropriateExplanation: A pathway with a smaller activation-energy barrier can have a larger rate constant at the same temperature and prefactor.
explanation: Activation energy is the energy-scale parameter in the Arrhenius relation for a reaction pathway.
Ea can be inferred from the slope of ln k against 1/T: slope=−Ea/R when the Arrhenius approximation is valid. It is not the same as the reaction enthalpy or the net energy released.
A catalysed route can have a different effective activation energy; a real multi-step mechanism may not show one constant Ea.
scientificPrinciples: Ea can be inferred from the slope of ln k against 1/T: slope=−Ea/R when the Arrhenius approximation is valid. It is not the same as the reaction enthalpy or the net energy released.

records.title: Chemical equilibrium
records.subject: Chemistry
records.shortDescription: Chemical equilibrium is a dynamic state in which forward and reverse reaction rates are equal and macroscopic concentrations remain constant.
records.ageAppropriateExplanation: Particles keep changing both ways even when the amounts stop changing overall.
explanation: Chemical equilibrium is a dynamic state in which forward and reverse reaction rates are equal and macroscopic concentrations remain constant.
For this closed reversible first-order A⇌B model, d[B]/dt=kf[A]−kr[B], [A]+[B]=Ctotal and K=[B]eq/[A]eq=kf/kr. More complicated stoichiometries require different expressions.
Reversible reactions can approach the same equilibrium from either side under fixed conditions.
scientificPrinciples: For this closed reversible first-order A⇌B model, d[B]/dt=kf[A]−kr[B], [A]+[B]=Ctotal and K=[B]eq/[A]eq=kf/kr. More complicated stoichiometries require different expressions.

definitions.Dynamic equilibrium: Equal opposing rates with no net macroscopic change.

realLifeExamples: Reversible reactions can approach the same equilibrium from either side under fixed conditions.

records.title: Solubility
records.subject: Chemistry
records.shortDescription: Solubility describes the amount of a substance that can dissolve at specified conditions. This investigation focuses on a dilute gas dissolved in a liquid.
records.ageAppropriateExplanation: A liquid can hold more of some gases when the gas above it is at higher partial pressure.
explanation: Solubility describes the amount of a substance that can dissolve at specified conditions. This investigation focuses on a dilute gas dissolved in a liquid.

For the chosen dilute, nonreacting gas at fixed temperature, Henry’s law is Ceq=kH pgas. The approach C(t)=Ceq(1−e⁻ᵏᵗ) is a chosen well-mixed transfer model. Solid solubility and reactive gases need different descriptions.
Carbonated drinks illustrate pressure-dependent dissolved gas, but CO₂ chemistry and bubbles are more complex than this ideal dilute model.

records.title: pH
records.subject: Chemistry
records.shortDescription: pH is the negative base-10 logarithm of hydrogen-ion activity; dilute solutions are often approximated using molar concentration.
records.ageAppropriateExplanation: A change of one pH unit corresponds to a tenfold change in hydrogen-ion activity.
explanation: pH is the negative base-10 logarithm of hydrogen-ion activity; dilute solutions are often approximated using molar concentration.

This ideal 25°C strong-acid/strong-base dilution model includes water autoionization with Kw=10⁻¹⁴. For a strong acid of analytical concentration C, [H⁺]=(C+√(C²+4Kw))/2; it does not model weak-acid dissociation or nonideal activities.
A tenfold dilution of a sufficiently strong acid approximately increases pH by one before water autoionization becomes important.
scientificPrinciples: This ideal 25°C strong-acid/strong-base dilution model includes water autoionization with Kw=10⁻¹⁴. For a strong acid of analytical concentration C, [H⁺]=(C+√(C²+4Kw))/2; it does not model weak-acid dissociation or nonideal activities.

definitions.Water ion product: Kw=[H⁺][OH⁻] in the ideal concentration approximation.

realLifeExamples: A tenfold dilution of a sufficiently strong acid approximately increases pH by one before water autoionization becomes important.
objectives: The model assumes complete strong-electrolyte dissociation.

detailedExplanation: Ionic crystals arrange positive and negative ions in extended structures with characteristic coordination.

The displayed NaCl fragment alternates equal numbers of positive and negative ions on a cubic grid and illustrates 6:6 coordination. Other ionic structures have different arrangements: CsCl has 8:8 and zinc-blende ZnS has 4:4 coordination; those structures are described but are not rendered by this NaCl model.
NaCl and MgO share the rock-salt structure type under suitable conditions; ionic size and energetics influence structural stability.

At large separation, attraction between a +e and −e ion is approximately Coulombic. At very short separation, electron-cloud overlap produces strong repulsion. The interactive curve combines a Coulomb term with an illustrative inverse-ninth-power repulsion chosen to have a minimum at 0.282 nm. This is an isolated-pair teaching model, not the total energy of a real NaCl lattice or a calculation of neutral-atom reaction energetics. Shells, electron positions and ion sizes are schematic.

records.title: VSEPR theory
records.subject: Chemistry
records.shortDescription: VSEPR uses repulsion among valence-shell electron regions to estimate the arrangements around a central atom.
records.ageAppropriateExplanation: Spread electron regions around a central atom, then look only at the atom positions to name the molecular shape.
explanation: VSEPR uses repulsion among valence-shell electron regions to estimate the arrangements around a central atom.

records.shortDescription: Neutralization is an acid–base reaction; for a strong acid and strong base in water, H⁺ and OH⁻ form water.

records.title: Radioactivity
records.subject: Physics
records.shortDescription: Radioactive decay is a spontaneous nuclear transformation; a population has a predictable exponential expectation even though individual decay times are random.

Radioisotopes are used as tracers and for dating when an appropriate decay model and calibrated half-life apply.

records.shortDescription: Relate shear stress to velocity gradient.
records.ageAppropriateExplanation: Dynamic viscosity quantifies the resistance of a fluid to shear and affects how quickly small particles settle.
explanation: Relate shear stress to velocity gradient.

A Newtonian fluid obeys shear stress η times velocity gradient. In this Stokes sedimentation example, radial settling speed is inversely proportional to dynamic viscosity η. The UI uses mPa·s and converts to Pa·s in the equation.
A more viscous carrier liquid slows the settling of the same small particles at the same rotor speed.

objectives: Relate shear stress to velocity gradient.

records.subject: Physics
records.shortDescription: Include both interacting carts.
records.ageAppropriateExplanation: Total momentum of a system remains constant when its net external impulse is negligible.

records.title: Density
records.subject: Physics
records.shortDescription: Use kilograms in the SI calculation.
records.ageAppropriateExplanation: Density is mass per unit volume and helps predict whether an object can float in a uniform fluid.
explanation: Use kilograms in the SI calculation.

Object average density is ρbody=m/V. In a free-floating static state, submerged fraction is ρbody/ρfluid when that ratio is below one. The bench uses a uniform rigid cube and excludes trapped-air changes, compression and surface tension.
A hollow steel vessel can have an average density below water even though solid steel is denser than water.

records.title: Continuity equation
records.subject: Physics
records.shortDescription: Compare two cross-sections of one steady stream.
records.ageAppropriateExplanation: The continuity equation expresses conservation of mass in fluid flow.
explanation: Compare two cross-sections of one steady stream.

For steady incompressible flow through a single pipe, volume flow Q=Av is constant between sections. Therefore v2/v1=A1/A2. In a circular pipe A=πr²; halving radius gives one quarter area and four times mean speed at fixed Q.
A hose nozzle can increase exit speed at a given volume flow; real supply flow may also change when a nozzle is fitted.

records.shortDescription: Water enters the plant according to water-potential gradients.
records.ageAppropriateExplanation: Water evaporates from leaves and is replaced by water moving through the plant.

Plants can lose more water in dry air than humid air under otherwise similar stomatal conditions.

detailedExplanation: Identify ocean, atmosphere, land and ice.

Evaporation, precipitation, runoff, melting and freezing move water between four model reservoirs. The numerical box model conserves their total water amount and uses prescribed rate coefficients; it is not a regional rainfall forecast or a complete groundwater model.
Rain falling on land can enter soils, rivers, groundwater or ice; this simplified model aggregates land water into one store.

Reservoir amounts change while their total remains fixed. Four well-mixed reservoirs, initial total 1000 relative water units. Linear transfers and numerical mass-conserving integration. Coefficients are teaching choices, not an Earth/climate calibration; no atmospheric energy or global water budget claim.

records.title: Moon
records.subject: Earth & Space
records.shortDescription: Sunlight lights approximately half the lunar globe.
records.ageAppropriateExplanation: The Moon’s visible phases depend on the Sun–Earth–Moon viewing geometry.
explanation: Sunlight lights approximately half the lunar globe.

Half the lunar globe is illuminated by the Sun at nearly all orbital phases, while the fraction of that illuminated hemisphere visible from Earth changes. In this circular coplanar phase model, visible illuminated fraction is (1−cosα)/2, where α is elongation measured from new moon.
A first-quarter Moon shows about half of its visible disc illuminated, not one quarter of the visible disc.

records.title: Seasons
records.subject: Earth & Space
records.shortDescription: The rotation-axis direction remains approximately fixed over a year.
records.ageAppropriateExplanation: Earth’s axial tilt changes solar angle and day length through the year, producing seasonal differences in sunlight.
explanation: The rotation-axis direction remains approximately fixed over a year.

The model keeps an inclined axis fixed in space while Earth follows a circular orbit. Solar declination, day length and top-of-atmosphere daily mean irradiance depend on latitude and season. Clouds, atmosphere, oceans and climate response are not calculated.
Northern and southern hemispheres have opposite seasons because their pole orientations relative to incoming sunlight alternate.

records.title: Planetary motion
records.subject: Earth & Space
records.shortDescription: The dominant mass sits at one focus of the ellipse.
records.ageAppropriateExplanation: Planetary motion under a dominant central gravitational mass follows Keplerian geometry to a useful approximation.
explanation: The dominant mass sits at one focus of the ellipse.

A bound ellipse has semimajor axis a and eccentricity e<1; a central body at a focus is swept out with constant areal velocity. For the fixed solar-mass units in this model, period in days is 365.256a^(3/2), with a in AU. Mutual perturbations are omitted.
A more eccentric orbit moves faster near perihelion and more slowly near aphelion.
scientificPrinciples: A bound ellipse has semimajor axis a and eccentricity e<1; a central body at a focus is swept out with constant areal velocity. For the fixed solar-mass units in this model, period in days is 365.256a^(3/2), with a in AU. Mutual perturbations are omitted.

definitions.Semimajor axis: Half the longest diameter of an ellipse.
definitions.Eccentricity: Dimensionless ellipse-shape parameter between zero and one for a bound ellipse.

records.formula: T² ∝ a³ for the same central mass; dA/dt = constant
realLifeExamples: A more eccentric orbit moves faster near perihelion and more slowly near aphelion.
objectives: The dominant mass sits at one focus of the ellipse.
Eccentricity changes closest and farthest distance.
The scene solves the ideal two-body Kepler problem.
misconceptions: An eccentric orbit does not move at constant speed; the constant quantity in Kepler’s second law is areal velocity.

records.shortDescription: The Sun dominates the solar system’s mass.
records.ageAppropriateExplanation: The solar system contains the Sun and bodies bound to it, including planets, moons, asteroids and comets.
explanation: The Sun dominates the solar system’s mass.

The original scene animates the eight planets using approximate sidereal periods with independently compressed body sizes and orbit spacing. It uses circular coplanar paths, illustrative rotation and procedural surface colours; it is not a scale model or current-position ephemeris.
The outer planets generally take much longer to orbit the Sun than the inner planets.
